title: FCC Approves SpaceX Plan for One Million Satellites to Power AI Data Centers in Orbit
excerpt: The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday authorized SpaceX to deploy up to one million satellites for orbital data centers — the first U.S. authorization of a space-based data-center constellation — raising both excitement about AI computing and alarm among scientists.
content:
The Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday authorized SpaceX to deploy up to one million satellites for data centers in space, the first U.S. authorization of a space-based data-center constellation and a regulatory win for Elon Musk’s plan to move artificial-intelligence computing into orbit.

The network, called Starmind, would be made up of one million orbital compute modules that process massive amounts of data in space for use on Earth, powered by solar energy captured in orbit and linked by high-bandwidth laser communications. The FCC said the constellation would help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing power.

SpaceX sought permission for the constellation earlier this year, filing its application on Jan. 30. The company already operates the largest satellite constellation ever assembled, with just over 11,000 Starlink satellites in orbit. A million-satellite Starmind network would increase the total number of satellites in Earth orbit many times over, and scientists have raised skepticism and alarm about orbital debris and the effect on the night sky.

The approval comes with a long leash and strict milestones. SpaceX must deploy its first operational Starmind satellite by November 2033, then 10% of the constellation — 100,000 satellites — by November 2035, and 50% by November 2038. The full constellation must be in orbit by 2040. SpaceX Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen said last week that the company plans to launch its first data centers into space in 2027 and expand through 2029.

The FCC did not approve every part of the plan. It declined, for now, the company’s request to move satellites operating above 600 kilometers into so-called graveyard orbits at the end of their lives instead of bringing them down to burn up in the atmosphere, and it has not yet approved SpaceX’s debris-handling plans for satellites above that altitude. In its ruling, the FCC maintained that the Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules. The satellites would fly at altitudes between 500 and 1,002 kilometers.

SpaceX is not alone in chasing the idea: Google and Blue Origin are pursuing orbital data centers of their own. For Texas, the decision lands close to home — SpaceX’s Starbase sits on the Gulf Coast, and the company’s launches from Texas have already made the state a center of the commercial space industry. Whether a million satellites ever actually fly is an open question; the approval is a license to try, not a launch manifest.
